span_text: Debbie and Chris Clarkson enrolled their first child, Lucas, at the Y's Learning Center almost four years ago. 'We were looking for a safe, supportive place for Lucas to learn, and after we took a tour of the Learning Center we knew that we'd found it,' Debbie says. 'You could see that it was a really established program with thoughtout and structured care. We were immediately impressed.' The Clarksons were so happy with Lucas' learning experience that when younger brother Everett came along, the decision to enroll him at the Learning Center was an easy one to make. Lucas is now in kindergarten and Everett, who just turned three, is in his second year at the Learning Center. He's made great friends in his class and loves being able to play with them every day. And both Everett and his parents have grown close with his Learning Center teachers, who they say bring a passion to the work that makes it obvious that it's not just a job to them. Last fall, both Debbie and Chris graduated from their respective programs at the University of Montana, which meant that they lost access to the Best Beginnings scholarship funds that they'd used to help pay for Everett's child care. Debbie reached out to Nanette Melzer, Learning Center director, and she worked with the Y's Member Services team to get the Clarksons set up with financial assistance. That assistance replaced some of the scholarship money they were no longer eligible for and helped make it possible for Everett to continue at the Learning Center and for Debbie and Chris to continue to work. 'It was a really stressful time, especially with it all happening right before the holidays,' Debbie says. 'But Nanette and her team had answers for us within a week. It was really amazing that they were able to do that so quickly and put us at ease.'

span_text: Desiree has been in foster care since she was three years old. Reaching her teen years with street-smart bravado and a history of sexual abuse, it was easy for her much-older boyfriend to convince her that prostitution was a viable alternative with the mythical allure of easy money. At just 17, she was being sexually exploited by him and, within a few months, she found herself pregnant and aging out of the group home where she lived. Desiree gave birth to a healthy baby boy, but, as a result of her time on the streets, she resented her son and wasn't sure she wanted to parent him. In June of 2013, Desiree moved into the Rising Oaks community, where she got the support and understanding she needed. The staff helped her find vocational training in which she was interested. Her Case Manager found respite services for her and her son, then accessed a slot for him in a supportive day-care program. In the midst of these positive supports, she was able to talk to her therapist about her ambivalence about both her baby and how she had come to be his mother. Through exploring these challenges, Desiree discovered a newfound commitment to parenting her son. Nine months after finding Rising Oaks, Desiree is successfully completing cosmetology training and is becoming more confident as a parent. She now believes she can provide her son with the family she lacked and that Rising Oaks has transformed two lives-her own and that of her son.

title: Background on domestic violence and homelessness
what_changed: No specific beneficiary story; general context.
span_text: According to the National Network to End Domestic Violence (NNEDV), domestic violence is one of the leading causes of homelessness for women and their children. Up to 57% of all homeless women report that domestic violence was the immediate cause of their homelessness and over 90% of homeless women have experienced severe physical or sexual abuse at some point in their lives. The lack of affordable housing, being unemployed, substance abuse and mental health issues are factors often recognized as root causes of homelessness in general. However, these experiences are often perpetuated by domestic violence. ' One major contributor to homelessness for domestic violence survivors is financial abuse. Financial abuse is present in 98% of abusive relationships ' A majority of survivors have been denied access to household funds, forbidden to work and/or had their credit and rental history sabotaged by their abusive partner. Financial abuse makes it extremely difficult for survivors to find a decent source of employment/income and to find landlords who will rent to them. This can leave survivors with the difficult choice of staying with their abuser or facing homelessness with their children. (familycrisisonline.org) There is also a shortage of available, affordable housing not just in our community, but all across the US. According to the National Low -Income Housing Coalition, an Idahoan working at minimum wage ($7.25/hr) has to work 72 hours a week to afford a one -bedroom rental at HUD ' s fair market rent ($680/ month). In our area, 42% of the population is considered low to moderate income, earning less than the area median income. Severely cost burdened households are more likely than other renters to sacrifice necessities like healthy food and healthcare to pay the rent and to experience unstable situations like evictions or staying with/returning to their abuser. Survivors can and do qualify for HUD Section 8 Housing vouchers. Idaho HUD has a basic 12 18 month wait list and Washington can be a 2 -3 year wait. Getting on the list is easy, finding a place to stay in the meantime or staying with the abuser during that time puts the survivor in more danger from abuse and risk of homelessness. The survivor is still responsible for finding a place that will accept Section 8 and a landlord who will agree to rent to them, which according to NNEDV, can take around 6 -10 months.  Difficulty finding affordable housing means shelters are often full and have an average stay of only 60 90 days, which falls far short of the time it takes to find secure housing or come to the top of the list for Section 8. Survivors of domestic violence often suffer from various mental illnesses directly relating to the abuse they have suffered. Anxiety, depression and PTSD are common among survivors, just to name a few. These disorders intensify difficulties in finding employment or housing and may result in behaviors that appear problematic to others. Survivors sometimes turn to substance abuse as a coping mechanism to deal with trauma. Substance abuse leads to addiction and other mental health issues. It makes it difficult to maintain or find employment and keep or find housing. Assistance can be hard to obtain, especially for underemployed or underinsured, and again, waitlists can be long, leaving time for an abusive situation to only get worse. Something that is not often discussed with substance abuse is coercion. Substance abuse coercion is another tactic an abuser uses to maintain control over their victim. This may include supplying and encouraging substance use or forcing their partner to use against their will without consent. Abusers may control when their partner has access to substances and force them into withdrawals as a way to cause harm and keep them in the relationship. Abusers may also use a survivor ' s substance use to justify the abuse or make the survivor think it never happened. They may threaten to turn their partner in to child protective services or the police if they leave. ' Substance use coercion creates major barriers to safety and recovery for domestic violence survivors, limiting their ability to engage in services and achieve health, well -being, and economic self -sufficiency ' (National Center on Domestic Violence, Trauma, and Mental Health). To address the problem of homelessness in our area and our country, it is important to raise awareness about the intersection of domestic violence and homelessness in order to promote early intervention and support for at -risk individuals. Support your local domestic violence agency, such as the YWCA, through donations, volunteering your time, and referring those in need. Become educated in and support legislation that reduces housing costs and supports survivors. Contact members of Congress, asking them to pass a budget with increased investments in affordable housing, implement policies that address income inequality, and create more gainful job opportunities for low -income individuals. Last, but not least, don ' t forget to use your voice and vote in your local, state, and federal elections.

title: Collaboration mission description
what_changed: No specific beneficiary story; mission language.
span_text: Working Together To Build A Strong Community The YWCA ' s mission to empower women and eliminate racism guides our work every day. The mission of YWCA Lewiston -Clarkston also includes dedication to building a strong community. The key to contributing to a strong community is collaboration working with other groups and individuals to make positive change. YWCA staff participate in a variety of community groups that consist of representatives of many agencies and organizations who collaborate to work more effectively together. These teams go by many names Coordinated Community Response, Task Force, Sexual Assault Response Team all with the goal of working together to address domestic violence and sexual assault. Collaboratively we can provide safety and support to victims of these crimes while holding offenders accountable for their actions. InterAgency and Human Needs Councils throughout the region provide an opportunity to learn from representatives of other agencies what services are available in the community to assist those we serve. Collaborating to provide resources to an individual or family can help them find stable housing or employment opportunities that might not happen without agencies working together. Collaborating with survivors is the priority of our work. The journey to healing from the trauma of violence and abuse begins where the survivor is when they reach out to us. Advocates work with survivors to determine their individual needs, barriers they face, and provide support, information, and resources that might be available to meet those needs or overcome those barriers. Leadership at YWCA Lewiston -Clarkston works collaboratively, as well, to provide the internal resources needed to continue our programs and services. Our Co -Directors work closely together to manage the business of a non -profit organization while our Leadership Team collaborates to guide our programs and services. This model provides a strong foundation for agency operations and will ease future transitions in leadership at the YWCA. Empowering Women, Eliminating Racism and Building a Strong Community takes collaboration on many levels. We are grateful for all of those who collaborate with us to move our mission forward.

span_text: At YWCA Lewiston, ID -Clarkston, WA your contributions create meaningful change in the lives of those we serve. Donate in Person: If you ' re considering donating supplies or contributing financially to the YWCA, we welcome the opportunity to connect with you in person. title: Emma's story of pandemic hardship
beneficiary: Emma, a single mom with two girls
what_changed: Emma was called back to work and is striving to get back on her feet.
span_text: What a year it has been! Pandemic fatigue is real and all of us feel it. We're looking forward to masks being out and hugs being in, going to the movies regularly again, and seeing extended families gather around the table. For many of us, that's what a slow return to a new kind of normal will mean. Now imagine you are Emma*, a single mom with two girls. Emma had a good job and a decent apartment. Her 7-year-old was in school and her younger daughter in daycare. But last April her boss told her she would be laid off until the pandemic was over, or until business could safely resume. They hoped for July. July came and went. Emma heard, 'Maybe September.' Emma began to panic. Unemployment insurance helped, but it wasn't enough. A new job was impossible - a 2nd grader can't do school from home alone. Her landlord was patient, but soon her bills would have to be paid and her family's basic needs would have to be met. Emma turned to St. Vincent de Paul for help. 'I've never had to ask for help before,' Emma cried. 'I don't know where to turn or what to do.' Thousands of Dane County families looked to the Society of St. Vincent de Paul last year for help with basic needs and we quickly and safely adapted: 30+ We have a limited supply of COVID-19 vaccines that we are offering to our clients. We have already vaccinated more than 30. Doses HELPING OUR NEIGHBORS IN NEED Michelle lives at Seton House. Donor support allows us to provide housing for men, women & children. Our shopping-style food pantry became a drive-through, still allowing families to use dollars that would have paid for food for rent or other bills. The charitable pharmacy moved curbside, giving life-saving medications to adults with low incomes and no insurance. Even flu shots were offered through car windows! Clients like Emma received vouchers to shop at our thrift stores for clothing, household goods, and furniture. Emma was finally called back to work and is striving to get back on her feet. She will continue to use our services for the time being. 'To the people who give to St. Vincent de Paul, I can't thank you enough,' Emma says.

title: Amanda's Wraparound Program success
what_changed: Amanda stabilized emotionally, attends school, completed second grade, started third, made friends, and the Wraparound case was closed.
span_text: A girl in the third grade (whom we will call 'Amanda') has spent three years in Phoenix Houses of Los Angeles' Wraparound Program. Coming from a very troubled family background, she was suffering from severe anxiety, not socializing and unable to attend school. Her case saw a lot of twists and turns. Initially, she survived a failed unification with Mom, then she survived a failed unification with Dad. The abandonment by parents negatively and severely impacted her mental health. She was so anxious that she did could not go to school, resulting in problems with her education as well. After enrollment in Wraparound Program to prevent her placement in foster care, 'Amanda' received individual therapy for a long time, but her mental state was not improving. Wraparound Approach means that the child and her family receive comprehensive services from a team- a Youth Specialist provides mentoring and advocacy to the child; a Parent Partner offers support and advice to the parents or caretakers; and a Therapist's professional efforts help stabilize and improve the child's mental health issues. A Coordinator ensures that all family issues are resolved and the child benefits from remaining at home, in a stable and welcoming environment. But 'Amanda' did not receive love at home and was anxious and unable to function due to her abandonment by parents. Finally, Grandma volunteered to care for the child, but then legal battles ensued, making 'Amanda' even more anxious and troubled. The main problem was that Grandma was unemployed and did not have enough money to support the girl. To resolve this issue, Phoenix House Wraparound Program staff initially offered Grandma flex funds for urgent necessities such as rent, food, and clothing. Staff then helped Grandma find and keep  a stable job. Consequently, the adoption paperwork could be completed, and Grandma became the legal guardian of the girl. Since moving in to her Grandparents 'Amanda' is doing much better. Her therapist reports that she is stabilizing emotionally, because her living circumstances are stabilizing. She attends school, completed the second grade, and started the third. In addition to succeeding academically, she has become far less socially anxious; she even made some friends at school! Therefore, the Wraparound Case was closed and she has been enrolled in Phoenix House Mental Health Outpatient Program to continue individual therapy she needs to function at home and school. After several years of participating in the Wraparound Program, 'Amanda's' life has stabilized, she was able to successfully return to school, catch up with education credits, and even to socialize with her friends.  This case shows how much effort is needed and how long it takes to help a youth abandoned by parents.

Over 50 CATA artists participate in CATA's seven different performing ensembles in dance, juggling, singing, drumming, and acting. CATA's Annual Performance is a major community event, drawing 800+ people to Shakespeare & Company each year. CATA partners with 24 schools across 9 districts, reaching 400 young people with disabilities annually. CATA begins partnering with the Clark Art Institute with a sixweek exhibit of work by artists with disabilities. span_text: When Cathy, a Council on Aging health coach, met Jack, he  had  recently  come  home  from  the  hospital  where he had undergone a femoral artery bypass. The surgery removed a blood vessel from his right arm and grafted it into his right leg to restore circulation that had been lost to vascular disease. The purpose of Cathy's visit was to help Jack avoid an unnecessary and costly return to the hospital. But the situation didn't look good. 'I could see he was in a lot of pain,' Cathy said. 'His incision sites were red and there was edema in his right arm and leg.' A former auto body repairman who has had plenty of scrapes from jagged metal, Jack shrugged these things Jack, COA Care Transitions client off.  'I've got a high tolerance for pain,' he said. 'It only hurt when I moved.' But  it's  precisely  that  attitude  that  made  Jack  a  good  candidate  for  Council  on  Aging's  Care  Transitions program.  The program uses trained health coaches, such as Cathy, to visit at-risk patients in their homes soon after hospital discharge. Their job is to empower patients to manage their conditions and connect with their doctors to prevent a revolving door to the hospital, a far too common experience for individuals on Medicare - and expensive for taxpayers. Their tools are basic, but effective, including medication management, keeping a Personal Health Record, and involving the primary care physician as soon as possible after discharge. In her visit with Jack, Cathy saw red flags all over the place. Because he had left the hospital on his own, without a formal discharge, he had no pain medication and no arrangements for skilled in-home services, such as a nurse and physical therapy.  Cathy also learned that he was lenient in his diabetes control and had not yet met with his primary care doctor. With Jack's permission, Cathy made a referral to a skilled nursing service for further wound care, medication management, diabetes education, and physical therapy.  When she called him a week later, he had seen his doctor, received antibiotics and pain medications, had his arm and leg wrapped to control swelling, and was undergoing physical therapy. Nearly two months later, he had not returned to the hospital and was doing much better.  At one time resigned to his health problems, he saw hope returning to his life. 'Before, I never checked my sugars (for diabetes control), but now I do at least once a day,' Jack said. 'It seems like I've got a lot more energy and I'm not out of breath as much. It used to be, if the doctor couldn't do anything for me, I just didn't care. It was like, why bother? Now, I feel like I want to try to do stuff. I want them to fix my left leg now.'

title: CEO letter overview
span_text: Letter from Chief Executive Officer About AGE of Central Texas Vision And Mission 2022 Impact 2022 Demographics 2022 Impact Data Program Update: Memory Connections AGE Expansion Update What a transitional year 2022 has been for AGE and all whom we serve! I love the saying 'Life isn't about waiting for the storm to pass, it's about learning to dance in the rain', and dance we have. However, we knew that 2022 was a pivotal year for our organization as we emerged from the most severe COVID restrictions and slowly moving towards a 'back to business' mentality. In 2022 we incorporated more digital programming based on feedback from our transition to providing digital services in 2020. We successfully adapted to make what we offer more accessible throughout the community. We also learned to balance the organization's need for forward movement with sensitivity around the collective trauma that society was still grappling following the pandemic. However, we didn't just survive: We learned to thrive knowing that we were able to continue serving those in need through COVID and devastating weather conditions. This only happened as a result of our community, amazing donors and funders who believed in us, and our own resilience and hard work. A sincere thank you to everyone who has kept AGE as a priority. In addition to the expansion, as caregivers started going back to work, our Thrive Social & Wellness Centers played an important role in offering exceptional programming for those who needed a loving, safe place for their care partner to land while they were working. We saw an increased need for our durable medical equipment program, HELP, and opened additional satellite locations outside of Austin to provide that needed support. Additionally, nothing was more needed than the spirit of community for our caregivers, so we responded by offering six conferences for caregivers available in-person and virtually, allowing family caregivers outside our geographic community to participate. On June 7th, 2022 our expansion efforts lifted off when we broke ground on a new state-of-the-art facility in South Austin. The building is going vertical and walls will be up soon! This dream is becoming a reality fast, and boy is it needed. I call our South Facility a beacon of hope for older adults and caregivers in the South Central Texas area who desperately need our services. Raising money during a pandemic has not been for the faint of heart, but we kept going. I look forward to sharing the facility with all of you. I could go on and on about our list of responsive solutions to the needs of our older adults and caregivers. I am so proud of our staff, board and volunteers who never stopped, kept showing up, and provided a place of comfort and support for those who need AGE. Gratefully, Suzanne Anderson, Chief Executive Officer AGE of Central Texas

title: Organization description and mission
span_text: AGE  of  Central  Texas  is  a  leading  regional  nonprofit  delivering  services,  education,  and assistance  to  support  the  area's  rapidly  growing  population  of  older  adults  and  family caregivers. AGE provides six core programs - including the Thrive Social & Wellness Centers, the  longest-operating  adult  day  health  service  centers  in  Central  Texas  -  in  addition  to providing  caregiver  education,  early  memory  loss  support,  health  equipment  lending, resource information, and peer-based computer classes for older adults. AGE collaborates with  partners  across  Central  Texas  to  provide  services  to  more  than  3,000  individuals annually. Founded in 1986, AGE's services cultivate strength, compassion, and community. Thrive Social & Wellness Centers: Providing vibrant daytime care for older adults with physical or cognitive needs in the longest-operating licensed, non-residential Day Activity and Health Service Centers in Central Texas Information & Resource Center: Free personalized resource and information navigation, monthly caregiver support groups and educational resources family caregivers and older adults. CaregiverU: Free evidence-based caregiving courses for non-professional, family caregivers. Health Equipment Lending Program (HELP): Free, gently used durable medical equipment loans and hygiene products for low-income older adults. Memory Connections: A comprehensive online support program for older adults experiencing mild or early-stage cognitive changes, where participants take a proactive approach to maintaining their quality of life, with access to Central Texas' only source for Cognitive Stimulation Therapy. AGE Computer Lab: Technology education designed to empower older adults to utilize technology independently and to deepen their skills through social connection. AGE envisions a society where aging is a shared journey marked by connection, strength, and vitality, and the role of caregiving is supported through community, collaboration, and guidance. AGE of Central Texas helps older adults and family caregivers thrive as they navigate the realities and opportunities of aging and caregiving.

title: Memory Connections program description
span_text: Memory Connections is a comprehensive lifestyle and support program that empowers older adults to live well with cognitive changes. Participants may be experiencing subjective cognitive decline, have received a diagnosis such as Mild Cognitive Impairment (MCI), or an earlystage dementia such as Alzheimer's disease. In 2022, Memory Connections evolved and launched Cognitive Stimulation Therapy (CST), an evidence-based intervention designed to actively stimulate the brain and provide a social environment. AGE is excited to be the first organization to offer this unique service (developed at the University College of London) in Texas. AGE will continue evolving this program in 2023 to meet the needs of the community by launching the Trailhead Series. This series is designed to build confidence and encourage a brain-healthy lifestyle; caregiver support groups, daily enrichment activity schedule, and in-person meetup opportunities in tandem with ongoing, personalized support. Client feedback indicates a myriad of benefits from participating in this program while experiencing the early stages of memory loss. At this stage, it is crucial for participants to keep their mind active and engaged while learning practical approaches to help manage and improve daily life. Staying involved in meaningful pursuits and connecting with peers going through similar experiences creates a vibrant community that many would lose access to without the Memory Connections Program.

title: Expansion goals
span_text: Double the number of older adults and caregivers served by AGE. Make AGE programs more accessible to those in areas identified as an "aging services desert". Provide new programmatic space which will allow us to offer more programs at a single location as a one-stop-shop for care. Foster collaboration within the nonprofit sector to collectively identify long-lasting solutions to the challenges of our aging Central Texas community.

title: Groundbreaking event description
span_text: December 30, 2022 On June 7, 2023, AGE leadership, stakeholders, and community leaders gathered at 9400 Alice Mae Ln. in Southpark Meadows to break ground on AGE's new comprehensive state-of-the-artfacility. The new site is expected to double the number of older adults and family caregivers served by AGE, house AGE's largest Thrive Social & Wellness Center to date, licensed to serve 75 individuals a day, provide programmatic space for AGE's other five programs, and, true to the mission of its's founders, offer belowmarket-rate office space for other nonprofits. With the support of funders such as the St. David's Foundation, Anderson Foundation, and H-E-B, the project is well underway and is set to open the summer of 2023.

span_text: Luna, a bright and spirited 4-year-old, has come a long way in learning to manage her emotions. Using Conscious Discipline strategies, we helped her recognize her feelings and practice calming techniques like deep breathing, talking it out, or drawing for comfort. None of this happened in isolation. Luna's mom, juggling work and school, partnered closely with our team to bring the same emotional tools into their home. Together, we created the consistent, nurturing support Luna needed to thrive. Her journey is a powerful reminder of what's possible when families and educators work hand-in-hand to help a child grownot just in skills, but in self-understanding and resilience.

Each of the 10 staff volunteers will tell you it was a true team effort -- something they felt compelled to do.  Muriel Cypert, a Registered Nurse and Nurse Educator and Karen Kerendian, Director of Health Services, devised a plan and wasted no time in enlisting the support of the administration. Soon, they transformed a conference room into a bustling workshop staffed by employees from throughout the organization. Kerendian and six other colleagues brought in sewing machines from home, including Alicia Scotland, Pat Lamb and Amy LeRoy,  while some, like Melissa Martinez, even sewed from home. Everyone rummaged for fabrics and supplies, while Pat Lamb, LPN, teamed up with Karen to search online for mask patterns. Kerendian, known to the group as the 'sewing machine whisperer,' was on call as needed and kept the sewing machines running with help from YouTube tutorials. They collected shoe laces, fitted sheets and shirts, and recycled unused supplies in storage as well as fabric and elastic. Every headband in every dollar store was purchased so they would have elastic for straps. The maintenance department also pitched in by making clear plastic templates to help with cutting patterns, which sped up production. Over several months, the team evolved into a core group of four. Before long, men and women throughout New Hope Community and Select Human Services, Inc. proudly showed off their themed masks. span_text: Facing backward, Richard, a single-leg amputee, inches his way toward lunch in his wheelchair, using his hands to move the wheels and his right foot to push off.  A camouflage cap sits tipped on his forehead, and sunshine warms his back as Richard crosses the threshold into the airy, renovated space known as the Fireside Lounge. 'Morning, Richard!' A CNA pushes his chair the final few yards to his usual spot in the center of the dining room, where he gazes toward the floor-to-ceiling picture windows that stretch across the eastern side of the room. The number of residents who previously ate meals alone in their rooms but now dine in the Fireside Lounge has increased, according to Kim Jung, Director of The Health Care Center. She believes that the airy, homelike environment is inviting and contributes to residents' desire to eat in the community. It is this sense of community and building relationships with others that staff strive for each day. One quarter of older adults in the U.S. are socially isolated, a circumstance associated with a 50% increased risk of dementia and a significantly increased risk of mortality, according to The National Institute of Health. Simply put, opportunities to engage with others are critical. Murmurs of hello from the others at Richard's table compete with the clinking of dishes from those in the service kitchen at the opposite end of the room.  As dining staff plate the food, prepared in the main kitchen and kept warm in chafing dishes, the certified nursing assistants (CNAs) serve the residents. In the Fireside Lounge, Richard dines and enjoys life enrichment activities with other residents. The addition of the service kitchen ensures hot plates and food. Meals are prepared in a large kitchen an elevator ride and a long walk away. Prior to the renovation, the already plated meals were transported on tall carts from the main kitchen and served directly to residents without reheating. Now, dining staff  have  the  ability  to  keep  food  warm  in  chafing  dishes before plating and serving. The process is efficient, but not rushed. A few CNAs deliver meals, water, milk and coffee while others wander the floor, stopping here to ask if they can cut a sandwich and there to ask how someone's day is going. 'Hi Marilyn, Hey Frank,' one woman calls out as she walks by. Tunes by Eric Clapton and Lionel Richie play softly in the background,  and  in  between  making  her  rounds  with  the residents,  one  CNA  breaks  out  in  a  short  dance  before continuing on, humming as she stops to assist a resident. This scene looked very different a year ago, prior to Project Revitalization, the $9 million building improvement. The renovation  touched  every  corner  of  campus,  including  the Health  Care  Center.  In  addition  to  the  expansion  and improvement of The Fireside Lounge, a grant from the City of Wauwatosa led to the redesign of the outdoor space adjacent to the Health Care Center, now known as Magnolia Garden. Other redesigned spaces include the nurses' station, offices for nurse managers, and a medication room. Kathy Jastromski, Health Care Center Life Enrichment Manager, talks to a resident while preparing an activity in the Fireside Lounge. With the rejiggering of the space in the Health Care Center, 'more  eyes  and  ears  are  on  the  residents,'  Kim  says.  ''Y ou can more easily see if someone has a change in condition or somebody isn't eating. There's more awareness of what's going on,' she adds. Back in The Fireside Lounge, lunch winds down, and Kathy Jastromski,  Health  Care  Center  Life  Enrichment  Manager  shows up to prepare an activity. She and others like Pastor Stephen Marsh facilitate opportunities outside of meals for connection and social interaction. Kathy uses the service kitchen to bake with  residents.    They  also  use  the  space  for  arts  and  crafts activities, games, movies, and musical entertainment. Pastoral Care offers prayer services and Bible studies. A dining services staff member plates the food (or boxes it for those who eat in their rooms) in the newly added Health Care Center service kitchen. 'I think the whole space welcomes engagement,' Kathy says. As residents wait for the activity to begin, they listen to music and watch staff cleaning up. One resident pulls out a deck of cards and begins a game of Kings in the Corner. Another watches the squirrels and rabbits outside. Richard's gaze turns upward. 'Three - that's the third one today!' he announces as a small plane soars above, heading toward nearby Timmerman Airport. The planes bring back memories --- three decades serving in the Marines and Air Force, tours in Korea and Vietnam, and even a job as a young man working at Timmerman Airport as a security guard. 'I like the scenery,' Richard says. 'I love watching the airplanes.'

span_text: One damp morning in April, Chimere checked on 'Helen,' who had fractured her foot.  Surgeons  had  attached  an  external fixation, or metal frame, to the outside of the foot for support during the healing process. Chimere observed that the external fixation had shifted. After identifying that the skin was warm to the touch and beginning to discolor, Chimere suspected an infection. Meanwhile,  Chimere's  day  grew  busier  with  admissions, discharges and more residents to evaluate. 'It's  busy  back  here  (the  2900  hall  of  short-term  care).  Y ou have the most admissions and the most discharges. Y esterday we had one discharge, two admissions and sent two people to the hospital,' Chimere said. Mary, a certified nursing assistant, responds to an alert on her phone from a resident needing assistance. Making efficient use of time is essential. In 2024, Luther Manor added AI-assisted modules to Point Click Care, their electronic medical  records  system.  The  upgrade  expedites  Chimere's tasks,  especially  during  admissions.  Providing  prompts  as she enters information on a patient, the system quickens the pace. For example, if a patient answers yes when asked if they smoke, the system will automatically guide Chimere through a smoking evaluation to determine the person's smoking habits and predict possible agitation from withdrawal. While juggling the day's admissions and discharges, Chimere needed  to  swiftly  address  what  was  later  confirmed  as an  infection  in  Helen's  foot.  She  entered  the  results  of  her evaluation of Helen in PCC, information that is read by nurses on other shifts, the nurse practitioner, and the medical director. Similar  to  auto-correct  on  a  smartphone,  AI  assistance  also works as a communication tool. 'It helps you articulate a little bit better what's going on with the resident,' she said. Following  this  communication,  the  medical  team  decides whether  a  hospitalization  is  needed  or  if  the  change  in condition  can  be  managed  by  the  nursing  staff.  Ultimately, Chimere  sent  Helen  back  to  the  hospital  for  treatment. Chimere's training and judgment led to the identification of Helen's  infection.  However,  in  other  cases,  AI  can  help  with the early detection of a patient's change in condition. While doing patient evaluations and entering information into PCC, recommendations pop up on her screen. After completing an evaluation of a patient on the short-term rehabilitation floor, Chimere, licensed practical nurse, uses her laptop to enter notes in Luther Manor's electronic medical records. to all areas of the Health Care Center. At the beginning of their shifts, Chimere and the other nurses and CNAs pick up smartphones, a part of the system. When a resident presses their call button for assistance, an alert pops up on the phones while a light turns on above the resident's door. Previously, CNAs were assigned to particular residents. If a call light went on and that CNA was busy with another resident, the first resident would need to wait. Now, when an alert flashes across the smartphones, anyone who is out of eyeshot of the light but available can answer the alert on their phone. Third Eye, a telehealth system, is another update. Used on weekends  and  at  night  across  campus,  physicians  respond virtually  within  a  few  minutes  of  a  call  being  placed  by  a  Luther Manor nurse. The system relieves Luther Manor's doctor and nurse practitioner who previously remained on call during all off hours. 'When you're doing your skilled evaluations, it will prompt you on what to look for and what to do. Y ou can catch it (a change in condition) before it happens,' Chimere said. In effect, the update can work as an early alert system that can lead to quick interventions,  possibly  preventing  further decline and helping avoid hospitalization. span_text: Grace* is an outgoing seventeen-year-old. Her friends call her 'Cover Girl' because she dreams of becoming a cosmetologist. Just a year ago, Grace was often angry, acting out socially and emotionally, due to trauma she'd suffered as a child. Grace didn't know her mom, who struggled with addiction and was incarcerated when Grace was a toddler. She was raised by a dad who loved her, but who also struggled with anger issues. Her father remarried, but Grace admits, even as a young child, she didn't make it easy. Then her stepmom left the marriage when she was only six years old. Grace felt she was responsible. 'They got along great,' she said, 'except when it came to me. They always seemed to argue.' Though her father dated other women, the relationships were too brief for Grace to create a real connection. She began sneaking out of the house and hanging with other troubled kids. After an outburst in her classroom, Grace was expelled from her high school. Her father sent her to a residential home in Orlando, but she returned within a month because 'they couldn't help her.' It wasn't long before Grace and her father had an explosive argument, during which he struck her. Grace called the police and her father was arrested. She was taken from her home and sent to live with her older sisters in Tampa. Unable to get along there, Grace ran away with a friend, spending the night walking around the city in bare feet. Her father continued to reach out to her, saying that he loved her and hadn't given up on her.  He told her he had found a place called HomeSafe and thought it might help her heal emotionally. When Grace arrived at HomeSafe, she admits it was hard at first, but eventually she made a close friend and connected with her therapist, who helped Grace get to the root of her anger and recognize her self-esteem issues. One year later, Grace has a plan to get her life back on track. She understands that she has control of her decisions and the ability to make healthy choices. Grace is now an A-student and has more confidence and self-awareness. She feels ready to rejoin her dad and her dog, Blue, in Kentucky where she can spend time fishing and riding dirt bikes. Grace is encouraged that her dad has also benefited from anger management therapy. She says she is happy for 'the first time in forever' and states, 'If I play my cards right and do what's best for me, I know I'll be alright.' She told us recently that she has also been able to visit with her biological mom, who has re-entered society and is in recovery. Grace said they just sat on the couch eating ice cream together… something she always wanted.

title: Founder reflection on growth
span_text: 2021 Annual Report 4,590,000 Diapers and Counting As Philip and I start our tenth year of doing this work, we are reflecting on how this passion project has grown over the last nine years. At the end of 2021,  we  hit  a  milestone  we  could  have  never  dreamed  of.  Since  Western Pennsylvania Diaper Bank's founding in 2012 we have distributed 4,590,000 diapers! The  last  two  years  have  been  very  challenging  but  we  did  it  with  your support. We have distributed millions of diapers and helped thousands of families in our communities. We have moved our warehouse space from a church basement (and survived a fire!) to 9,000 square-feet in two locations, Point  Breeze  and  Mt.  Pleasant,  to  better  serve  families  in  three  counties. Some of our volunteers are now staff, and our volunteer network continues to  grow  to  include  students  and  dedicated  corporate  and  community partners. We would not be where we are today if it was not for our partner agencies,  donors,  volunteers,  foundations,  and  friends  believing  in  our mission and values. We are doing this work together. Our goal is to continue helping individuals of all ages with essential needs, from  diapers  to  menstrual  products  and  incontinence  supplies.  As  the Diaper Bank grows, I'm growing with it and taking advantage of learning opportunities through PACE, Bayer Center, Forbes Funds, Full Circle-Social Venture Partner (SVP) and others. Thank you to our Board of Directors who work  hard  to  raise  awareness  of  the  diaper  crisis  in  our  region  and supporting the many families we serve. Thank you to everyone that has supported us throughout the last nine years! Your dedication enables us to serve our community. Cathy Battle

span_text: The last thing that Rebecca needed was two feet of water in her basement. But on August 11th, 2014, that's exactly what the busy mother of six found in her Oak Park home after a rainstorm for the ages hit our region. Her husband was in between jobs, and keeping up with the needs of six children is a challenge for any family. Fortunately, at the most desperate moment, Jewish Family Service was there to help. Rebecca learned that JFS was providing assistance to families affected by the flood from an email circulated by community leaders, and she met with JFS staff within days of the storm during special hours at the Oak Park JCC. In short order, JFS helped Rebecca buy cleaning supplies, hired a crew to sanitize the basement, and replaced damaged furniture, appliances and other essential items. Unfortunately, the flood itself was just the beginning of a complicated ordeal for the family. Once the water finally receded, a contractor concluded that the home's foundation was saturated during the storm. The whole home was in danger of collapse, and Rebecca and her husband were facing a monumental expense. Fortunately, JFS was there to help once again. JFS helped negotiate a manageable rate for the foundation repair, provided a $5,000 grant for a down payment, assisted with FEMA paperwork, and connected Rebecca with partners at Hebrew Free Loan to secure the remaining needed funds. A caring, supportive caseworker was present throughout the process to help Rebecca manage the many dimensions of the crisis. 'Finally, just a couple of weeks ago, we had all the work finished. My basement is dry now,' Rebecca said. 'When things are at their most desperate, I turned to JFS and said, 'I'm stuck,' and they helped. It's an amazing thing.'

span_text: There are 19,000 children in the foster care system in Florida. Unfortunately, too many of them have experienced the trauma of abuse or neglect. Living in these conditions, it is no surprise that they have great difficulty managing their emotions and behavior. HomeSafe's first newly-constructed campus offers twelve children their own private suite, an open living space, therapy and educational wings, and a teaching kitchen. HomeSafe is the only organization in South Florida equipped to provide the high level of therapeutic care and support that these children need. We are one of five organizations in the entire state that is accredited to provide the intensive therapy program these children require to heal their hurt, including passionate caretakers and therapists, enrichment and educational opportunities, and wholesome, safe, and secure accommodations.

title: Suzanne Wright stays in apartment until death
what_changed: Suzanne was able to remain in her Bethesda Gardens apartment with her belongings until she passed away, avoiding a move during declining health.
span_text: After her mother's health started declining in March 2012, Janet said the ability for her mother to remain in her apartment made a big difference in the quality of life in her final days. Suzanne passed on Feb. 20, 2013. 'We were able to keep her where she had made a lot of friends so that, when she was able to be social, she was surrounded by people, she could get to the dining room or have visitors there,' Janet said. 'Moving her at that point in her health and age would not have been ideal.' Her mother was able to remain in her beloved Bethesda Gardens apartment thanks to Bethesda's Geriatric Care Management program, a service offered through Bethesda Senior Support Solutions that benefits residents and members of the community by providing free counseling and coordination of care. When staff members at Bethesda Gardens realized that Suzanne's health was starting to decline, they got in touch with Chandelle Martel, Bethesda's Geriatric Care Manager and one of a few certified professionals in St. Louis who specialize in coordinating and planning care for seniors. After consultations with Suzanne and her family, a team from St. Andrews & Bethesda Home Health started providing therapy and home care. Janet worked with Chandelle to transition the care over to Bethesda Senior Support Solutions once Suzanne's coverage under home health lapsed. 'Chandelle spent a lot of time with me and my siblings explaining the options we had and what things we should have in place, conversations we should have with our family,' Janet said. 'We started talking to her 18 months before my mom passed away. And she just gave us good direction through the whole process.' After Suzanne received a terminal diagnosis from her physician, she continued with Bethesda Hospice Care until she passed away. Janet's goal had been achieved-Suzanne had been able to stay in her apartment, with her beloved Renoir painting and walls painted in her favorite shade of blue.

title: Letter writing reflection
span_text: How do I begin writing a letter that truly reflects the last 12 months? Do I share the good, the bad, and the ugly? I decided to go with the truth of what this last year has offered, its challenges, and how we have continued to serve.

title: Retirement of Michelle Schiller-Baker
span_text: On December 31st 2019, Michelle Schiller-Baker retired after 38 years of service. Each and every one of us at St. Martha's Hall stands on her shoulders. We miss her daily and look forward to her weekly cards that make us laugh, and sometimes cry, but always inspire.

title: Residents overcoming pandemic challenges
what_changed: Families quarantined, managed virtual school, secured jobs while healing from trauma.
span_text: I watched the unprecedented events of this year bring residents to their knees. Every time they chose to get back up and continue the fight, not just against the violence in their lives but also against a global pandemic. Families have quarantined in shelter for 7-14 days, maneuvered virtual school despite technical difficulties, been patient with ever-changing shelter guidelines, and still managed to secure jobs. All while healing from a lifetime of pain.

title: Staff challenges and dedication
span_text: The staff of St. Martha's Hall has not been immune to trauma. Each and every one of our staff members has battled their own tragedies, from COVID-related deaths in their family to accepting the risk to their own health by showing up to work every single day. Or by working from home because they are on the kidney transplant list and can't risk getting sick. And crises that have nothing to do with the pandemic but are equally heartbreaking. The staff of St. Martha's Hall is second to none when it comes to compassion and dedication. They serve no matter the cost.

title: Gratitude for community support
span_text: Despite quarantines, isolations, and social distancing, we have never been surrounded by more love and generosity. We have felt that support through your donations of homemade masks, your purchases of tshirts that supported us while also supporting local businesses, your gifts of cookies, your calls and emails to check on staff and residents, and your prayers. I thank each and every one of you from the bottom of my heart.

title: Year-end reflection and hope
span_text: This year has been tough, but the residents, staff, and supporters of St. Martha's Hall have been tougher. I look forward to welcoming 2021 and celebrating the hope a New Year promises.

title: Prayer for justice
span_text: 'May God bless you with anger at injustice, oppression, and exploitation of people, so that we may work for justice, freedom, and peace'.

title: Holiday wishes and signature
span_text: On behalf of the entire staff I wish you a happy, healthy holiday season. Jessica Woolbright Executive Director

title: Mission statement
span_text: Our mission is to help abused women and their children break the cycle of violence in their lives.  St. Martha's Hall is guided by the social justice teachings of Jesus Christ.

title: Trauma-informed care integration
span_text: In July of this year we began the process of integrating our knowledge about trauma into policies, procedures, and daily practice. Counselors from St. Louis Counseling provided us with the support needed to recognize the signs and symptoms of trauma in the families we work with and in staff. Identifying the far-reaching effects of trauma assists in developing plans to heal and build resilience against future trauma.

title: History and services description
span_text: Since  1983  St.  Martha's  Hall  has  been  providing  confidential  emergency shelter and support services to abused women and their children. We provide a supportive environment with a strong emphasis on peer support; implement a self-help philosophy to enhance self-esteem and decision-making skills;  provide  accurate  information  and  referrals  to  abused  women  and  their children  and  when  appropriate  to  their  abusers;  provide  advocacy  services; provide individual, group and family counseling; and offer community education to increase public awareness and understanding of domestic violence.

title: Court Watch Project update
span_text: Despite the challenges these past several months, the St. Louis Ending Violence Against Women Network (SLEVAWN) Court Watch Project continues to be an integral part of the advocacy work within the domestic violence victim service community. Since the beginning of the pandemic, the Court Watch Project Coordinator has organized a group of advocates and stakeholders from multiple organizations to coordinate a network of communication. This network is instrumental in providing updates regarding procedural changes in the St. Louis City and St. Louis County courts.

title: New employee introductions
span_text: We are happy to welcome three new employees.  Melanie, our Children's Program Coordinator, originally started with us 8 years ago as a volunteer. Eldisa, the Children's Advocate, brings with her 9 years of domestic violence experience. Theresa was hired as an Advocate and has extensive experience as an administrator at WashU.  She brings a unique and straightforward perspective to her work with the families at St. Martha's Hall.

title: Tax credit and donor list info
span_text: Saint Martha's Hall is a registered 501(c) 3 non-profit agency.  All donations to Saint Martha's Hall are tax-deductible. The Missouri Department of Social Services offers a special Domestic Violence Shelter Tax Credit equal to 50% of the amount of a donation.  St. Martha's Hall offers this tax credit to any cash donation of $250 or more over and above the value of goods and services received.  The amount of the credit cannot exceed your state tax liability for the taxable year, but if it does, it can be carried over for four successive years. This report honors donors who have made contributions during the July 1, 2019 - June 30, 2020 fiscal year. We have tried to make this list accurate but we do make mistakes.  If your name has been omitted,  misspelled or incorrectly listed please notify Lauren Alvino at 314-533-1313 or laurena@saintmarthas.org.

title: Statistics and numbers
span_text: Support and information to 1,878 callers through the 24-hour crisis and support hotline. 39 support groups 23 parenting support groups for women 70 support groups for children. Assistance for 51 women establishing a goal plan for their lives freed from abuse . Peace, safety, and hope for 4,982 days and nights. Resources to build for the future through 1,329 referrals to other services for our residents. Continued support and resources through follow-up services to 52 women. Support, information and accompaniment for 14 women going through the judicial system.

title: Survey results on safety and hope
what_changed: 100% know more ways to plan for safety; 95% know more community resources; 100% feel more hopeful; 100% of mothers report children can manage emotions.
span_text: The Family Violence Prevention and Services Act, which is part of larger federal legislation, provided funding to develop nationally standardized surveys to help document the work of domestic violence organizations.  The two key survey questions that are used at St. Martha's Hall ask:  As a result of staying in our shelter do you know more ways to plan for your safety and do you know more about community resources? 100% of the women responding said they know more ways to plan for their safety and 95% said they knew more about community resources. 100% of the women stated that they feel more hopeful about the future as a result of their stay. 100% of mothers completing a survey regarding their children stated that they can identify, manage, and appropriately express their emotions and behaviors as a result of their stay.

title: Prayer by Sister Jeanne Meurer
span_text: 'Spirit of the Holy One may you guide and inspire all at St. Martha's Hall to be Protectors of the women and children sheltered there and that all women and children in our community are afforded safety and shelter. I ask a special blessing for all at St. Martha's Hall, the women, the children, the staff, the volunteers and the Board of Directors. May they be blessed with a deep abiding peace for their love, care and safety that they provide to the women and children at St. Martha's Hall.' -Written by Sister Jeanne Meurer, FSM

title: Tribute to Sister Jeanne Meurer
span_text: This year we said goodbye to our dear friend Sister Jeanne Meurer. Those who were fortunate enough to work alongside her saw first-hand the strength and tenacity she embodied when advocating for the safety and wellbeing of women and their children. Sr. Jeanne held a Master's in Nursing Administration from St. Louis University, a Master's in Maternity Nursing from Columbia University, and a Master's in Theological Studies from Aquinas Institute. She assisted in establishing nurse-midwifery as a profession and in 1972 opened the first nurse-midwifery service at City Hospital. Under a World Health Organization fellowship, she studied maternal nursing in Denmark, Sweden, and Norway.   Sr. Jeanne was instrumental in opening Cardinal Glennon Children's Hospital in 1956. Throughout her career in the medical field, Sr. Jeanne continued to learn, teach and inspire the next generation. After almost two years of working to identify the gaps in domestic violence services, she co-founded Woman's Place, the region's only drop-in center for domestic violence victims.  She worked tirelessly to improve the community's response to those experiencing violence in the home and reducing the impact on children.  Sr. Jeanne was known to persuade and motivate even the toughest of critics.

title: Covills rely on transit for 25 years
what_changed: The Covills continue to stay connected to their community and maintain their active lifestyle through reliable transit service.
span_text: For over  25  years, Ron and Winnie Covill relied on Cimarron Transit to participate in life. Their journey with the CPTS began in November of  1999, in Ponca City. The active couple regularly scheduled outings to community meetings, events as well as trips to medical appointments, senior center and stores. In  2024, Ron and Winnie moved to Cleveland, Oklahoma-but their commitment to Cimarron Transit never wavered. Today, The Covills continue to use CPTS, staying connected to their community, appreciating the friendly drivers, dependable rides, and the peace of mind that comes from years of reliable service.

title: Ron Covill praises life-changing transit
what_changed: No concrete change stated; only sentiment and praise.
span_text: 'Winnie and I have been riding with Cimarron Transit over the past  25  years, said Ron Covill. 'I am totally blind and my wife, Winnie, has impaired vision, as well. Cimarron Transit has been life-changing for us. The staff and drivers are all very courteous and willing to help anytime needed. We are very appreciative of the service Cimarron Transit offers and we would be lost without their services.'

stage2_reason: Harper Phillips is a specific beneficiary; the change is from not babbling to speaking and now reading at grade level with college prospects, an observable sustained improvement.
title: Harper's early intervention leads to success
what_changed: Harper received speech therapy at age one, began speaking after dance class, and now reads at grade level in eighth grade with college prospects.
span_text: In 2010, Kerissa and her husband, Clint, welcomed their first child, Harper, who was able to attend Early Head Start alongside her mother. Despite Kerissa's training and expertise, it was not apparent that her own daughter might be experiencing a developmental delay. It was Harper ' s Early Head Start teacher who first approached Kerissa with a concern: although Harper was meeting most developmental milestones, she wasn ' t babbling - an early sign of communication difficulties. Thanks to early intervention, Harper began speech therapy at just one year old. By the time she turned three, Harper was still behind in her speech development; an unexpected breakthrough came when Mom, (Kerissa), enrolled Harper in a dance class. Dance, to the family ' s surprise, helped stimulate Harper ' s brain development, and the toddler began speaking. Later, as Harper entered public school, she was diagnosed with dyslexia and provided adaptive equipment. Now in eighth grade, Harper reads at grade level, competes in dance competitions, twice performing with the Tulsa Ballet. ' Harper still receives support services, '  Kerissa shares,  ' and due to early intervention, she will be able to go to college. I credit the Early Head Start teachers in Stillwater for being so observant and supportive. They made all the difference. '

stage2_reason: Emily is a specific beneficiary, and the passage describes a concrete change in her self-confidence and a notable achievement (singing at an Astros game) resulting from the program.
title: Emily's Miracle League transformation
what_changed: Emily's self-confidence grew immensely, she blossomed, and she was invited to sing the national anthem at a Houston Astros game.
span_text: Our daughter Emily was diagnosed with Autism at the age of three. When she was younger, we had a difficult time finding any type of team sport that she could participate in. Then, I read about The Miracle League in a newspaper article and contacted the Y.  Little did I know how much that phone call would change our lives. At first, Emily was shy and very hesitant to even leave the dugout. As she became more comfortable, she was invited to sing the national anthem before the game, and her life changed forever. Her self-confidence grew immensely and she was blossoming right before our eyes. She was ultimately invited to sing the national anthem at a Houston Astros game, which was one of the biggest highlights of her life. Before The Miracle League, her world was very small and limited. After, her self-confidence grew such that she was able to feel more comfortable and confident in a world that is not always kind to people who are different. One thing we know for sure, she wouldn't be the person she is today without The Miracle League and all of the wonderful volunteers that make this program such a bright light in a sometimes dark world. For that, we will always be eternally grateful.

title: ForeverWell participant's first camp
span_text: 'This is my first time to Camp Cullen and my first trip to camp in my lifetime. I enjoyed the activities. Most of what we did was a first for me and the outing was very interesting. I always thought Camp Cullen was only for kids. Thank you for allowing us this experience. The staff and volunteers at camp were helpful and very friendly. I will surely visit again next time when you organize. Thanks again for all your efforts in making this event a great success.' -YMCA ForeverWell Participant PETZL

title: Habib's swimming lesson praise
span_text: 'Until a few weeks ago, I was terrified of water and did not know anything about floating and swimming. YMCA's swimming lessons helped me a lot in learning the skills and confidence to be safe in water. I've improved very well since the first day. I enjoy swimming and it eases my mind.'

title: Athziri on computer classes
span_text: 'I started computer classes about a year ago and it's been great. I like when we work with Tinkercad because we can build many things. I also like robotics because it's a lot of fun, we do contests and I like to win, and if I lose I keep trying. Kodable, we do it to make patterns for the game so that the characters can move and beat the game.'

title: Teen on StrongHER program
span_text: 'I really enjoyed StrongHER because it made me feel safe in being me! Social media really does play on your mental health and often makes you really believe that what you're seeing on the Internet is reality. StrongHER reminded me that I'm beautiful and I'm powerful and I can do anything that I put my mind to. I also appreciated being around other girls that struggled with similar issues and the way we supported each other and formed positive relationships.' -YMCA Teen

span_text: Shaniqua knows about what it's like to lose the things you love.  But she also knows  what  it's  like  to  be  loved.    She's  encountered  seemingly  countless obstacles.  And she knows what it's like to overcome them.  She entered foster care a week before her 12th birthday. And she was adopted the week before her 18th birthday.  She was devastated at the death of her first foster parent, Deborah Thrower, and thankful to have found the mother that adopted her, Star Pierce. Shaniqua  is  currently  a  senior  in  high  school  with  a  3.6  GPA.  She  is  3rd  in her  class,  .2  points  away  from  being  Salutatorian,  and  for  her  graduation she is going to have the biggest open house and is going to invite her entire 'Orchards' family'. She will be attending Central Michigan University in August, living on campus and studying Sports Management with dreams of becoming a sports agent. Shaniqua recognized early on the importance of education.  'It's important to make your own money… Legally that is!' she said. Shaniqua has been an active member of the Orchard's Youth Group, spoke at a youth conference held at Orchards in February and participated in overnight camps through Orchards Summer Adventures.  Shaniqua says that she has learned the following things about herself from her life experiences thus far:  how to be a leader, how to be loyal, that she cares for others, that she is a very independent person.  When asked what advice she has for other kids in foster care, Shaniqua stated, 'Have your own mind, follow the house rules, stay out of trouble, set VERY high goals for yourself by finishing high school and going to college, do not let anyone put you down and prove yourself. '  Shaniqua represents the power, hope and determination in every young person, and serves as a shining example for us all.

span_text: Anvil  (pronounced AN-VEE-EL) came to Orchards at age 12 along with five siblings.    Their  father  was  absent  from  the  home,  contending  with  serious behavioral  issues.  Their  mother  had  become  gravely  ill,  was  hospitalized, and upon returning was unable to care for her children due to her medical condition.    All  of  the  youth  were  placed  in  foster  care.  With  the  assistance of Orchards Kinship Care program, Anvil and her siblings were reunited with their biological father in Genesee County.  Formally, the case was 'closed' as a success.  But the story doesn't end there… Despite many obstacles, Anvil successfully graduated from high school intent on becoming a nurse.  And in October of 2008, she reached out once again to Orchards, having learned we had developed a program to support older youth who had 'aged out' of foster care in Genesee County.  Anvil stated, 'Orchards helped me before, I know you will help me out again.'  She began working with  her  'Youth-In-Transition'  support  staff,  attended  the  Orchards  holiday party and participated in Orchards Adopt-A-Family program.  Her dedication and determination recently paid off when Anvil learned she had been accepted into the Job Corp program.  She is a resident student studying to become a Certified Nursing Assistant and a Dental Hygienist.  Anvil's story reminds us that, even from tremendous adversity, the greatest success can blossom.

span_text: Summer of 2017 I was accepted to the Heroes and Horses program for Veterans with PTSD.  As a retired Navy Chaplain with 29 years of service I have helped many suffering with the affects of Trauma however, it was all too easy to overlook my own wounds and issues.  When I retired I felt disconnected and a bit lost.  I felt that I had lost my tribe of fellow military members who I had a connection and understood me. Having the time to reflect and incorporate the lessons that the horses and the Heroes and Horses team was offering has allowed me to reconnect with the inner strength and examine the issues that combat trauma has played in my life.  Many of my significant relationships, particularly my wife and children, have noticed a big change.  I'm more connected, engaged and don't check out when faced with challenging life circumstances.  Heroes and Horses was and continues to be a tremendous source of strength, resiliency and hope. - Will, 2017 program graduate
